meta.unit: The sons of Mosiah among the Lamanites (Alma 17–26)
principles: Teaching from where the hearer stands

world_behind.title: The servants testify first
world_behind.text: Verse 1 has the king calling them to stand forth and report what they saw. Ammon says nothing for twelve verses. The case is made by the people he defended. Refusing the marriage offer is what put him among them.

world_behind.title: The scattering was an industry
world_behind.text: Verse 7 explains the practice at Sebus: scatter the flocks, drive off what disperses, keep it. It was "a practice of plunder among them" (v. 7), and the king's habit of executing the servants who lost animals made it profitable and safe.

cites.quote: a practice of plunder among them

spans.text: a practice of plunder among them

world_behind.title: Lamoni already had a theology
world_behind.text: Verse 5 says the Great Spirit was his father's tradition, and that believing in one had not stopped the people supposing whatever they did was right. Ammon arrives to a man with a word for God and no content behind it.

world_behind.title: The king had been killing his own servants
world_behind.text: Verse 4 has him say so plainly: the Great Spirit came so that he might not slay these as he did their brethren. His first religious thought in the chapter is about the men he executed.

world_behind.title: Rabbanah is a Lamanite word the record translates
world_behind.text: Verse 13 supplies it with a gloss, powerful or great king. The book rarely stops to translate. It does so here for a title given to a servant by another servant, at the moment Ammon's standing changes.

world_behind.title: The hour of silence is measured
world_behind.text: Verse 14 says the king answered nothing "for the space of an hour, according to their time" (v. 14). The qualifier tells the reader the Lamanites kept hours and that the abridger knew his own were different.

cites.quote: for the space of an hour, according to their time

spans.text: for the space of an hour, according to their time

world_behind.title: The teaching is a full course, compressed
world_behind.text: Verses 36 through 39 run from the creation and the fall through the records, the fathers' journeys, what Laman and Lemuel did against them, the plan of redemption, and the coming of Christ. The record lists the syllabus and quotes none of it.

words.text: A Lamanite title, given in their own language and then explained: "Rabbanah, which is, being interpreted, powerful or great king" (v. 13). It occurs nowhere else in scripture. A servant uses it of Ammon, who is also a servant, in front of the actual king. The record keeps the untranslated word and the gloss both. It does that when a term carries something the English will not.

cites.quote: Rabbanah, which is, being interpreted, powerful or great king

spans.text: Rabbanah, which is, being interpreted, powerful or great king

words.text: Wonderings, taken as a plural noun. The form appears twice, both in this chapter, and never in the King James Bible. Ammon asks "what is it, that thy marvelings are so great" (v. 17), turning the king's astonishment into a countable thing he can ask about. The oddness of the plural is the point: there were several wonderings, and Ammon wants the list.

cites.quote: what is it, that thy marvelings are so great

spans.text: what is it, that thy marvelings are so great

words.text: Doing no injury. Ammon is called "being wise, yet harmless" (v. 22), very nearly the pairing Christ gives his own missionaries when he sends them as sheep among wolves, wise as serpents and harmless as doves. The word occurs once in this record. It arrives four verses after the man it describes cut off a row of arms.

Craft, cunning in getting what one wants. The verse says Lamoni "was caught with guile" (v. 23), and Paul uses the same construction of himself with the Corinthians (2 Cor. 12:16). What Ammon actually did was ask a question and receive a promise, which the king gave freely. The record uses a word that sounds like trickery for a bargain struck in the open.

Hard labor, and in the King James Bible usually the labor of childbirth or of the soul. Treated at 2 Nephi 29:4. Here it belongs to the fathers in the wilderness, listed with hunger and thirst. Ammon is telling a Lamanite king the story of Lehi's journey, and he counts the suffering of the people this king's ancestors abandoned.

To set out at length, to explain a text. Ammon "expounded unto them all the records and scriptures" (v. 38), and the verb governs the whole teaching section. It implies a text in hand and a listener being walked through it, a different activity from preaching.

cites.quote: expounded unto them all the records and scriptures

spans.text: expounded unto them all the records and scriptures

phrases.term: Whether he be the Great Spirit or a man, we know not
phrases.text: The servants report the limit of their knowledge before reporting what they do know. It is careful testimony from frightened men, and the carefulness is what makes the rest credible to the king.

phrases.term: This was the tradition of Lamoni, which he had received from his father
phrases.text: The record explains the king's belief and its source in one line, then notes what the belief had failed to do. Tradition is the word this book uses for what the Lamanites inherited, and Alma 9 said the same thing about the same people from the other side of the border.

phrases.term: It being a practice of plunder among them
phrases.text: The record names the scam plainly. What looked like random violence at the water was a business with a method, and the king's own executions were part of what made it work.

phrases.term: Rabbanah, which is, being interpreted, powerful or great king
phrases.text: A servant addresses another servant with a royal title, in the king's hearing, and nobody corrects him. The gloss is supplied for the reader. What the moment establishes is that the household has already decided what Ammon is.

phrases.term: The king answered him not for the space of an hour
phrases.text: Ammon asks what he can do for the king, and gets an hour of nothing. The record measures it. Lamoni is not being rude; verse 14 says he did not know what to say. The chapter's pace stops dead while a man works out what he is facing.
The narrator's assessment of Ammon at the moment he makes his one request. He asks Lamoni to hear him out before he explains anything, and the record labels the tactic as wisdom that does no harm.

phrases.term: I do not know what that meaneth
phrases.text: Lamoni's answer to whether he believes in God, and it is honest rather than hostile. He does not have the word. Ammon changes vocabulary instead of changing hearers, and asks about the Great Spirit instead.

Three words that carry the chapter. Ammon takes the term Lamoni already has and tells him it names the being Ammon is talking about. Everything after this is addition to a foundation the king brought with him.

phrases.term: He fell unto the earth, as if he were dead
phrases.text: The chapter ends mid-collapse. Lamoni has prayed for mercy on himself and his people, and then the record leaves him on the ground for two days. Nothing is explained until the next chapter.

verses.label: v. 3
verses.title: Servants who mark the limit of what they know
verses.text: The record gives the servants' testimony to the king a care nothing else in the chapter shows: "Whether he be the Great Spirit or a man, we know not; but this much we do know, that he cannot be slain by the enemies of the king." One claim is refused and another is asserted, and the line between them is drawn explicitly. The king's own conclusion in the next verse is less cautious than his servants': "Now I know that it is the Great Spirit."

verses.label: v. 13
verses.title: A title translated twice over
verses.text: The chapter stops to gloss a word: "Rabbanah, which is, being interpreted, powerful or great king." Being interpreted is used in four verses of the whole volume, at 1 Ne. 17:5, Alma 31:21, Alma 37:38 and here. This one is unusual among the four because it offers two renderings rather than one, joined by or, which is what a translator does when no single English word will carry the term. Rabbanah stands in this verse alone.

verses.label: v. 14–16
verses.title: Two questions and no answer, kept in the record
verses.text: The record has Ammon ask "What wilt thou that I should do for thee, O king?" and get nothing. He asks again, "What desirest thou of me?", and verse 15 reports the result plainly: "the king answered him not." A record could have moved straight to the conversation. Instead it preserves an hour of silence, and then explains it from the inside, since verse 16 has Ammon perceiving the king's thoughts and verse 18 has the king marvelling that he could.

verses.label: v. 22–23
verses.title: The record names its own hero's method
verses.text: Two descriptions sit three lines apart. The first borrows a phrase from Matt. 10:16, where the instruction is to be "wise as serpents, and harmless as doves": here it is "Ammon being wise, yet harmless." The second is blunter. After the king promises to believe whatever he is told, the record says: "And thus he was caught with guile." Guile stands in this verse alone in the whole volume. Its compound, beguile, appears at 2 Nephi 9:9, Mosiah 16:3 and elsewhere, and there it always belongs to the devil deceiving the first parents. This is the one place the shorter word is used, and it describes a missionary.

verses.label: v. 24–28
verses.title: The first question fails, and the failure is kept
verses.text: The record has the catechism open badly: "Believest thou that there is a God? And he answered, and said unto him: I do not know what that meaneth." The word does not translate. What follows is the repair, done in three short verses: "Believest thou that there is a Great Spirit? And he said, Yea. And Ammon said: This is God." A record that wanted a clean conversion would have started at the second question. This one keeps the term that failed and the substitution that worked.

verses.label: v. 36–39
verses.title: A syllabus listed and never quoted
verses.text: The record reports the teaching as a table of contents: he "began at the creation of the world, and also the creation of Adam," told him "all the records and the scriptures," rehearsed the journey of "their father, Lehi, from Jerusalem," then "the rebellions of Laman and Lemuel, and the sons of Ishmael," and finally "expounded unto them the plan of redemption, which was prepared from the foundation of the world." Five subjects, none of them given in the speaker's words. Everything Ammon actually said in this chapter is the dialogue; everything that persuaded the king is summarised.

chapter.title: Ammon says nothing for twelve verses
chapter.text: The chapter opens with other people testifying about him. His labor with the flocks and the horses argues first, and he begins speaking only when a servant fetches him. The order is the method.

chapter.title: The horses matter more than the arms
chapter.text: Verse 10 says the king marveled more at Ammon preparing the chariots than at the fighting, because the order predated the crisis. Routine obedience where nobody was watching is what actually moves him.

chapter.title: The teaching starts inside the hearer's vocabulary
chapter.text: Lamoni does not know what God means and does know what the Great Spirit means. Ammon does not correct the term or explain why it is inadequate. He says this is God, and builds from there.

chapter.title: Belief is assembled in pieces
chapter.text: Creation of the earth, yes; heavens, unknown. Ammon supplies the heavens, then who is in them, then what he sees and knows. Each answer becomes the ground for the next question, and no step is skipped.

chapter.title: The record calls a fair bargain guile
chapter.text: Ammon asked for a hearing and got a promise, in the open, with the king's consent. The word guile puts a reader on alert and the facts do not support suspicion. Paul described his own conduct the same way.

chapter.title: The syllabus is listed and the sermon is withheld
chapter.text: Four verses name everything Ammon taught and quote none of it. The record has given this material at length elsewhere and here spends its space on the man hearing it.

chapter.title: The king's prayer is for his people before it is finished
chapter.text: The whole prayer is one sentence at verse 41: "O Lord, have mercy; according to thy abundant mercy which thou hast had upon the people of Nephi, have upon me, and my people." Three features stand in it. It cites a precedent, and the precedent is the mercy shown to the nation his people have been at war with. It asks for himself and for his people together. And it makes no confession and no promise. Alma 22:18 has his father pray the same way a chapter later, offering "all my sins to know thee" but asking nothing for himself beyond knowledge.

applications.title: Do the thing you were told before the crisis
applications.text: Ammon is found "feeding thy horses" and preparing the chariots, an order given before any of the trouble started. The king's astonishment at verse 10 is about the faithfulness rather than the miracle. Being reliable in the standing assignment is what makes the unusual moment legible.

applications.title: Let the silence run
applications.text: Ammon asks what the king wants and gets nothing for an hour, asks again and gets nothing again. He does not fill the gap with talking. When someone cannot answer yet, waiting is a form of respect that is easy to lose patience with.

applications.title: Say the plain thing about yourself
applications.text: Offered awe, Ammon declines it in nine words, "Behold, I am a man, and am thy servant." When somebody overestimates you, correcting it early costs less than being found out later.

applications.title: Ask for the hearing first
applications.text: Ammon's one request was that the king listen, "Wilt thou hearken unto my words, if I tell thee by what power I do these things?" Secure the attention before spending the material, and ask for it as a favour rather than assuming it.

applications.title: Change your vocabulary, not your audience
applications.text: "Believest thou that there is a God?" draws "I do not know what that meaneth," so Ammon asks about the Great Spirit and gets a yes, then says, "This is God." Find the word the person already has and build from there.

applications.title: Attribute the power and keep the limit
applications.text: Ammon says a portion of the Spirit dwells in him, giving knowledge "and also power according to my faith and desires which are in God." The claim is large and bounded in one sentence, and both halves are said out loud.

applications.title: Start at the beginning when the beginning is missing
applications.text: Having found agreement on one point, Ammon "began at the creation of the world" and worked forward. Somebody who lacks the frame does not need a better argument; they need the earlier chapters.

applications.title: Pray for your people in your first prayer
applications.text: The king's whole prayer is one sentence and it asks for two parties, "have mercy... upon me, and my people," citing what was done for the Nephites as the precedent. The first thing he does as a believer is intercede for a nation.

questions.text: When I testify about something I saw, do I mark where my knowledge stops?
What do I believe that has never yet changed what I think is permissible?
What would someone find me doing if they came looking for me right now, and what would it tell them?
When did I last let a silence last as long as it needed to?
What have I dismissed as unbelief in someone that was actually just an unfamiliar word?
Ammon answers "who are you" with "I am a man." What would I have said, and why?
When I finally ask for mercy, whom else do I ask it for?
